identification.bodyShape: Long, torpedo-shaped body with a flattened, shark-like head profile, a protruding lower jaw, and a single long-based dorsal fin.
identificationTraits: Broad, flattened head with a shark-like silhouette that leads to frequent misidentification as a shark from a distance.
Single long-based dorsal fin, unlike the sucker-disc dorsal fin of its closest living relative, the remora.
Lower jaw protrudes slightly beyond the upper jaw.
Juveniles show alternating black-and-white horizontal stripes with patches of bronze, orange, and green; this patterning is lost in adults, which become uniformly dark brown to silver-brown.
identification.coloration: Dark brown to silver-brown overall as adults, with a paler belly and no strong body pattern once mature.
identification.juvenileAppearance: Boldly patterned with alternating black-and-white horizontal stripes and patches of bronze, orange, and green.
identification.adultAppearance: Uniform dark brown to silver-brown, torpedo-shaped, with the diagnostic flattened head and single long dorsal fin; juvenile banding is gone.

similarSpecies.name: Remora / sharksucker (family Echeneidae)
similarSpecies.distinction: Cobia's closest living relative; remoras have a modified sucker disc on top of the head where cobia instead has a normal long-based dorsal fin, and remoras stay much smaller.

similarSpecies.name: Small coastal sharks (various)
similarSpecies.distinction: Cobia's flattened head and dark, uniform coloration cause frequent confusion with sharks at a distance, but cobia have a single long dorsal fin set well back on the body and lack visible gill slits along the side.

identification.averageAdultLength: A sourced population-average length was not found; legal minimum sizes (roughly 33–40 in depending on jurisdiction and sector) mark the lower end of typically retained fish.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal fish start around 33–40 in depending on jurisdiction and sector; many landed fish are well under the documented maximum size.
identification.typicalWeight: A sourced population-average weight was not found; fish over about 50 lb are generally considered large.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 6–6.5 ft (roughly 2 m) and up to about 100 lb.
identification.longevity: Documented to roughly 12 years in one NOAA source; this record does not attempt to resolve other longevity estimates in the wider literature.

gaps: No sourced population-average length or weight — only maximum size and legal minimum sizes were found, hence status: partial.
Regional common names (e.g. ling, lemonfish) were not confirmed against an acceptable source and are omitted rather than guessed.
Detailed fin-spine count and other meristic identification traits were not found in an acceptable source.

social.byLifeStage: Adults travel alone or in small groups rather than large schools.
social.note: Frequently associates with large free-swimming animals — sharks, sea turtles, and rays — as well as with fixed structure, rather than schooling with conspecifics.

feedingStrategy.note: Strong, aggressive predator; feeds mainly on crustaceans (notably crabs) but also takes fish and squid.

dielTendency.note: Not clearly sourced by time of day; classified as mixed pending a source-backed determination rather than left blank, since the field is required.

behavior.depthMovement: Ranges from shallow bays and inlets to the edge of the continental shelf depending on season and life stage, tracking bait and temperature rather than holding a fixed depth.
behavior.coverUse: Strongly structure- and object-oriented — buoys, floating debris, wrecks, artificial reefs, and large free-swimming animals (sharks, turtles, rays) all draw cobia.
behavior.openWaterBehavior: During migration, cruises along the beachfront and over nearshore/inner-shelf water, often near the surface, rather than holding to a single piece of structure.
behavior.seasonalActivity: Strong seasonal migrator: moves south and offshore into warmer water in late fall and winter, then back north and inshore as water warms in spring, producing the well-known spring nearshore migration on the Atlantic coast that is commonly sight-fished from small boats along open beaches.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Multiple-batch spawner over an extended spring-through-summer window on inner-to-mid continental shelf water; this record excludes specific spawning and staging locations as conservation context only.

diet.primaryNote: Strong, aggressive predator feeding mainly on crustaceans, especially crabs, with fish and squid also taken. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.adult: Crabs and other crustaceans predominate, with fish and squid also taken.

diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity described here is not proof of a current feeding event; what cobia are actually eating on a given day still has to come from direct observation.
gaps: Juvenile and young-of-year diet not found in an acceptable source, hence status: partial.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Cobia's calendar is dominated by a strong temperature-driven migration: north and inshore along the Atlantic coast as water warms in spring, offshore and south again as it cools in fall. This produces the well-known spring nearshore sight-fishing period on the Atlantic coast. Regulatory season length is separate from this biological pattern and changes yearly with quota status.

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore and inshore water along the coast, cruising near the surface as it moves north and inshore with warming water; structure use includes buoys, channel edges, and bridges.
entries.movementTendency: Peak of the northward and inshore migration on the Atlantic coast.
entries.thermalContext: Movement tracks warming water; field-observed adult range runs roughly 19.6–28.0°C depending on region and season.
entries.presentationImplication: Flats sight cast and run-and-gun cast to sighted cruising fish inshore and nearshore; structure pitch at bridges and channel edges.
entries.conservationNote: Spawning begins in this window on the inner-to-mid shelf in at least part of the range; specific sites and timing are excluded from this record.

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore and offshore shelf water; continues holding near structure and cruising near the surface.
entries.presentationImplication: Live-bait slow troll and tide-line drift along weed lines and current rips offshore; run-and-gun cast to sighted fish nearshore.
entries.conservationNote: Documented spawning continues into this season, particularly for Gulf populations.

entries.habitatClass: Begins moving south and offshore toward warmer water.
entries.presentationImplication: Tide-line drift and live-bait slow troll along nearshore and offshore structure and current edges.

entries.habitatClass: Concentrated in warmer southern/offshore water for the Atlantic stock; Gulf fish shift toward south Florida from the northeastern Gulf.
